name: Gas turbines (heavy-duty)
description_md: With interconnection queues at five years and nuclear a decade out, gas turbines are the only dispatchable generation that can be added on data-center timescales — and all three global makers are sold out for roughly half a decade. GE Vernova's gas-turbine backlog plus slot reservations hit 116GW in Q2-26 (~5 years of output; taking reservations for 2031 delivery; expects ≥125GW by year-end), with ~20% explicitly for data centers. Siemens Energy has ~87GW on the books (60GW firm orders + 27GW reserved) with waits up to four years inside a record €154B group backlog. Mitsubishi Heavy's contracts are running at more than double the prior pace and it is doubling manufacturing capacity. Buyers now pay for reservation slots before contracts — an option market for turbines. Status basis: judged binding — 4-5-year committed order books at all three suppliers make near-term incremental gas power essentially unbuyable, pushing buyers to gensets, fuel cells (Bloom's ~$7.65B of DC contracts in 90 days), and aeroderivative stopgaps.

controlled_by.share_note: ~40-45% of heavy-duty GT market; 116GW backlog+reservations ≈5 years of output (disclosed)
~87GW order book (60 firm + 27 reserved), up to 4-year waits (disclosed)

dependents.dependency_md: Behind-the-meter gas campuses (Abilene/Stargate lineage) are built around turbine availability; slot access is the business model's core input.
Colossus (Memphis) runs on dozens of on-site gas turbines; expansion requires either new slots or secondhand/mobile units at premium prices.
Stargate-class campuses need firm on-site or contracted gas power on 2026-28 timelines only turbines (or fuel-cell substitutes like its 2.8GW Bloom agreement) can meet.
IPP expansion (e.g., $4.7B gas-fleet purchase) is partly a bet that existing turbines are worth more than new ones that cannot be delivered before ~2030.

substitutes_md: For firm power on <4-year timelines: aeroderivative turbines and reciprocating gensets (Caterpillar backlog +92% to $72B; Cummins), fuel cells (Bloom Energy — Oracle 2.8GW master agreement, ~$7.65B of DC contracts in 90 days), mobile gas fleets (VoltaGrid), and buying existing plants (Vistra's $4.7B fleet purchase — repricing scarcity, not adding capacity). Renewables+storage substitute energy but not 24/7 firmness for dense AI load. All substitutes are more expensive per firm MW; the queue for large frames is effectively unjumpable before ~2029-30.
downcycle_md: Order books look bombproof but contain soft layers: 'slot reservations' (27GW of Siemens' 87GW; a large share of GEV's 116GW) are fee-backed options, not full contracts — in a demand fall they simply expire, deflating backlog headlines without equivalent revenue loss. Firm utility orders (the majority) survive on regulated-capex logic even if AI demand fades, since queues also serve reshoring/electrification. The exposed parties are the capacity expanders (MHI doubling, GEV/Siemens adding lines) if 2029-30 deliveries land into a glut, and speculative DC-power intermediaries holding slots they cannot re-sell. Historical analog: the 2000-01 turbine bubble, when US orders collapsed ~90% and GE Power took a decade to recover — the reason all three makers are expanding cautiously and demanding reservations fees this time.
